name: Saul's rash oath, and the people at the blood
charge: A rash oath that snared the army; the people eating flesh with the blood; the son who unknowingly broke the oath
summary: Saul adjured the people to eat nothing until evening, and the army fainted in the pursuit. Jonathan, who had not heard, ate honey; the people, famished, fell on the spoil and ate with the blood; and when the lot fell on Jonathan the people would not let the king kill the man who had wrought the day's salvation.
offense: Jonathan went against the Philistine garrison trusting that the Lord could save by many or by few. The attack was followed by trembling throughout the host and the enemy turning its swords against itself (1 Samuel 14:6-23). In the midst of that deliverance, Saul placed the army under a curse against eating until evening, so that he might be avenged upon his enemies (1 Samuel 14:24). His added command deprived the pursuing men of strength. Honey lay within reach, but the people feared the oath. Jonathan, who had not heard it, tasted honey and was refreshed. When told, he said his father had troubled the land and that the army could have done more had it eaten (1 Samuel 14:25-30). The distinction matters: he had not knowingly broken a charge he heard. Saul's command had nonetheless brought the deliverer himself within the danger of the curse. The famished people fell upon the spoil and ate with the blood (1 Samuel 14:31-33). Their hunger did not repeal the commandment. Leviticus 17:10-14 forbids eating blood because the life of the flesh is in it. A ruler's imprudent burden and the people's unlawful response both belong to the history; correcting the one did not make the other righteous.
judgment: Saul was told, The people sin against the Lord, in that they eat with the blood, and he rolled a great stone and had the beasts slain on it, and built his first altar. Then the Lord answered him not, and the lot taken to find the cause fell on Jonathan. Saul swore he should surely die; the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not, on the witness that he had wrought with God that day. The oath was Saul's; the mercy was the people's; the silence was the Lord's.

entries.commentary: Jonathan said unto the young man that bare his armor, Come, let us go over to the Philistines' garrison on the other side; but he told not his father. Saul tarried under a pomegranate tree in Migron with about six hundred men, with Ahiah the priest wearing an ephod, and the people knew not that Jonathan was gone.

Between the passages were two sharp rocks, Bozez and Seneh, one facing Michmash and the other Gibeah. Jonathan said, Come, let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised; it may be that the Lord will work for us: for there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few. The Lord put that spirit on Jonathan. That is how the Most High operates: he loves to show his power by having a small number defeat a very large number. That is why it will be the 144,000 taking over the whole world; that is just how he rolls.

His armor bearer said, Do all that is in thine heart: behold, I am with thee according to thy heart. Jonathan set the sign: we will discover ourselves unto them; if they say, Tarry until we come to you, we will stand still in our place; but if they say, Come up unto us, then we will go up, for the Lord hath delivered them into our hand. That is how they would know the Lord had given the green light.

Both of them showed themselves to the garrison, and the Philistines said, Behold, the Hebrews come forth out of the holes where they had hid themselves; and the men of the garrison said, Come up to us, and we will shew you a thing. The sign came to pass exactly; the Lord had delivered them into the hand of Israel. Jonathan climbed up upon his hands and upon his feet, his armor bearer after him, and that first slaughter was about twenty men within about half an acre of land. Two men against a garrison. Some hold a doctrine that Jonathan was a homosexual; this act answers it. Scaling a rock face to rush a garrison two-deep is a bold, manly act of war that most men are not cut out for; he carried himself like a real man.

There was trembling in the host, in the field, and among all the people; the garrison and the spoilers also trembled, and the earth quaked, so it was a very great trembling. The Philistines got caught off guard and panicked. The watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude melted away, and they went on beating down one another; in their panic and confusion the Philistines started beating on each other.

Saul numbered the people and found Jonathan and his armor bearer missing. While Saul talked with the priest, the noise in the host of the Philistines went on and increased, and when Israel came to the battle, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture; the enemies were destroying each other, and Israel did not have to put in the work. The Hebrews that were with the Philistines from the country round about turned to be with the Israelites that were with Saul and Jonathan, and the men of Israel which had hid themselves in mount Ephraim followed hard after them in the battle when they heard the Philistines fled. So the Lord saved Israel that day, and the battle passed over unto Bethaven.

Saul had adjured the people, saying, Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies; so none of the people tasted any food. Saul put out a strange order, and the men of Israel were distressed that day. All they of the land came to a wood, and there was honey upon the ground, and the honey dropped, but no man put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath. But Jonathan heard not when his father charged the people with the oath; he was not there when the order came out.

Jonathan dipped the end of his rod in an honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes were enlightened; like the first taste after a long fast, he felt like a whole new creature. Then one of the people told him his father straitly charged the people with an oath, and the people were faint. Jonathan said, My father hath troubled the land: see how mine eyes have been enlightened, because I tasted a little of this honey; how much more, if haply the people had eaten freely of the spoil of their enemies, had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines? He began to convince the people that eating was the better idea and that the king's order was folly.

They smote the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very faint. Then the people flew upon the spoil, took sheep, oxen, and calves, slew them on the ground, and did eat them with the blood; too faint to prepare the meat, they ate it raw with the blood, and that was the transgression Jonathan's talk led the people into. When they told Saul, he said, Ye have transgressed: roll a great stone unto me this day; bring every man his ox and his sheep, slay them here, and eat, and sin not against the Lord in eating with the blood. And Saul built an altar unto the Lord, the first altar that he built unto the Lord.

Saul proposed going down after the Philistines by night to spoil them until morning, and the people agreed; then said the priest, Let us draw near hither unto God. And Saul asked counsel of God, Shall I go down after the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into the hand of Israel? But he answered him not that day. If you are spiritual, when the Lord ignores you, you understand at that point what it reveals: it is sin. It has to be; the scriptures give only that reason.

Saul said, Draw ye near, all the chief of the people, and know and see wherein this sin hath been this day; for as the Lord liveth, which saveth Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die. But there was not a man among all the people that answered him. Saul said unto the Lord God of Israel, Give a perfect lot; and Saul and Jonathan were taken, but the people escaped. Then they cast lots between Saul and Jonathan, and Jonathan was taken. Jonathan told him, I did but taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in mine hand, and, lo, I must die. And Saul answered, God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan. Saul was ready to kill his own son over the oath.

The people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not; they kept him from the wrath of his father. Think about the contrast, and why the scripture says to get the love of the congregation. In chapter 13 Saul was the one disobeying the voice of the Lord and getting rebuked, while Jonathan was brave and mighty and had just saved Israel out of the hand of its enemies; now the coward wants to kill the deliverer. In some situations you have to weigh it like the people did: yes, he made a mistake and crossed the order, but he just saved all our lives.

Saul took the kingdom over Israel and fought against all his enemies on every side: Moab, the children of Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines; and whithersoever he turned himself, he vexed them. He gathered an host, smote the Amalekites, and delivered Israel out of the hands of them that spoiled them. The chapter closes with his house: his sons Jonathan, Ishui, and Melchishua; his daughters Merab and Michal, whom we will learn about later; his wife Ahinoam; and Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle, captain of his host. There was sore war against the Philistines all the days of Saul, and when Saul saw any strong man or any valiant man, he took him unto him.

*1 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 2 Speak unto Aaron, and unto his sons, and unto all the children of Israel, and say unto them; This is the thing which the LORD hath commanded, saying, 3 What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp, 4 And bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, to offer an offering unto the LORD before the tabernacle of the LORD; blood shall be imputed unto that man; he hath shed blood; and that man shall be cut off from among his people: 5 To the end that the children of Israel may bring their sacrifices, which they offer in the open field, even that they may bring them unto the LORD, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, unto the priest, and offer them for peace offerings unto the LORD. 6 And the priest shall sprinkle the blood upon the altar of the LORD at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, and burn the fat for a sweet savour unto the LORD. 7 And they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils, after whom they have gone a whoring. This shall be a statute for ever unto them throughout their generations. 8 And thou shalt say unto them, Whatsoever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers which sojourn among you, that offereth a burnt offering or sacrifice, 9 And bringeth it not unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, to offer it unto the LORD; even that man shall be cut off from among his people. 10 And whatsoever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among you, that eateth any manner of blood; I will even set my face against that soul that eateth blood, and will cut him off from among his people. 11 For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul. 12 Therefore I said unto the children of Israel, No soul of you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger that sojourneth among you eat blood. 13 And whatsoever man there be of the children of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among you, which hunteth and catcheth any beast or fowl that may be eaten; he shall even pour out the blood thereof, and cover it with dust. 14 For it is the life of all flesh; the blood of it is for the life thereof: therefore I said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall eat the blood of no manner of flesh: for the life of all flesh is the blood thereof: whosoever eateth it shall be cut off. 15 And every soul that eateth that which died of itself, or that which was torn with beasts, whether it be one of your own country, or a stranger, he shall both wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even: then shall he be clean. 16 But if he wash them not, nor bathe his flesh; then he shall bear his iniquity.* --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

Keep your foot when you go to the house of the Most High and be more ready to hear than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they do not consider that they do evil. Be not rash with your mouth nor let your heart be hasty to utter anything before the Most High, for he is in heaven and you upon earth; therefore let your words be few. This means watch your mouth, which is why Christ said you will give account of every word. -

When you vow a vow to the Most High, do not defer to pay it, for he has no pleasure in fools; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, nor say before the angel that it was an error, lest the Most High be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands. This is what Christ meant by not swearing by heaven, earth, or your own head. -

If you see the oppression of the poor and the perverting of judgment and justice in a province, do not marvel, for he that is higher than the highest regards it, and there are higher than they. Do not worry about the wicked that are successful and all they are doing, because there is a God and that God will have his vengeance. This is why the scriptures say vengeance is his and he will repay. -

He that loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he that loves abundance with increase; this also is vanity. When goods increase, those that eat them increase. As one rapper said, more money more problems: the more money most people get, the bigger their family gets, meaning the more food you can buy, the more mouths there are to feed. The sleep of a laboring man is sweet whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich will not let him sleep. The rich lose sleep to gain wealth; ask successful entrepreneurs and businessmen and they work off four or five hours of sleep.

There is a sore evil under the sun: riches kept for the owners to their hurt, and those riches perish by evil travail so that the son is left with nothing in his hand. As a man came from his mother's womb naked, so shall he return, and take nothing of his labor to carry away in his hand. In all points as he came, so shall he go, and he has labored for the wind, eating in darkness with much sorrow, wrath, and sickness.

It is good and comely for a man to eat, drink, and enjoy the good of all his labor all the days of his life which the Most High gives him, for it is his portion. Every man to whom the Most High gives riches, wealth, and power to enjoy them and rejoice in his labor, this is the gift of the Most High. He shall not much remember the days of his life, because the Most High answers him in the joy of his heart. Ecclesiastes is a book of regret, and we can learn from it; in the end you see what really matters in this life. Money is a defense, but keep the commandments in the faith of Christ, which is what Solomon was saying. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)

verses.text: And the men of Israel were distressed that day: for Saul had adjured the people, saying, Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies. So none of the people tasted any food.
And all they of the land came to a wood; and there was honey upon the ground.
And when the people were come into the wood, behold, the honey dropped; but no man put his hand to his mouth: for the people feared the oath.

But Jonathan heard not when his father charged the people with the oath: wherefore he put forth the end of the rod that was in his hand, and dipped it in an honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth; and his eyes were enlightened.
Then answered one of the people, and said, Thy father straitly charged the people with an oath, saying, Cursed be the man that eateth any food this day. And the people were faint.
Then said Jonathan, My father hath troubled the land: see, I pray you, how mine eyes have been enlightened, because I tasted a little of this honey.
How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? for had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines?
And they smote the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon: and the people were very faint.
And the people flew upon the spoil, and took sheep, and oxen, and calves, and slew them on the ground: and the people did eat them with the blood.
Then they told Saul, saying, Behold, the people sin against the Lord, in that they eat with the blood. And he said, Ye have transgressed: roll a great stone unto me this day.

And Saul said, Disperse yourselves among the people, and say unto them, Bring me hither every man his ox, and every man his sheep, and slay them here, and eat; and sin not against the Lord in eating with the blood. And all the people brought every man his ox with him that night, and slew them there.
And Saul built an altar unto the Lord: the same was the first altar that he built unto the Lord.

And Saul said, Let us go down after the Philistines by night, and spoil them until the morning light, and let us not leave a man of them. And they said, Do whatsoever seemeth good unto thee. Then said the priest, Let us draw near hither unto God.
And Saul asked counsel of God, Shall I go down after the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into the hand of Israel? But he answered him not that day.
And Saul said, Draw ye near hither, all the chief of the people: and know and see wherein this sin hath been this day.
For, as the Lord liveth, which saveth Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die. But there was not a man among all the people that answered him.
Then said he unto all Israel, Be ye on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side. And the people said unto Saul, Do what seemeth good unto thee.
Therefore Saul said unto the Lord God of Israel, Give a perfect lot. And Saul and Jonathan were taken: but the people escaped.
And Saul said, Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son. And Jonathan was taken.
Then Saul said to Jonathan, Tell me what thou hast done. And Jonathan told him, and said, I did but taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in mine hand, and, lo, I must die.
And Saul answered, God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan.

And the people said unto Saul, Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the Lord liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day. So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not.
Then Saul went up from following the Philistines: and the Philistines went to their own place.

And whatsoever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers that sojourn among you, that eateth any manner of blood; I will even set my face against that soul that eateth blood, and will cut him off from among his people.
For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
Therefore I said unto the children of Israel, No soul of you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger that sojourneth among you eat blood.
Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.
For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool’s voice is known by multitude of words.
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
